data.description:

Dycom Industries (DY)

Dycom Industries is a specialty contractor that builds and maintains the fiber, telecom, and utility infrastructure that AI data centers depend on, linking it tightly to the construction and logistics wave behind the theme of this screener. The company generates essentially all of its roughly US$6.9b in revenue from Communications work in the United States, with a small segment adjustment. Dycom’s market cap is about US$9.1b, which places it firmly in mid to large cap territory.

Investors looking at the AI data center freight story may pay attention to Dycom Industries because it works on the physical fiber and power networks every large facility needs. The company has been building a sizeable backlog tied to long haul fiber, data center interconnects, and building systems work, which can support multi year project visibility and cash generation. At the same time, Dycom carries meaningful debt and runs on relatively thin profit margins, so any slowdown in customer spending or cost overruns on big projects could be a risk. For investors focused on the theme of AI infrastructure buildout, Dycom sits at an intersection of construction, logistics demand, and cash returns through buybacks that some may find worth a closer look.

AAON (AAON)

AAON designs and manufactures large HVAC systems, including dedicated data center cooling units, that have to be hauled by truck into construction sites during build and fit out. The business is anchored by AAON Oklahoma, which generated about US$1.1b of revenue, with AAON Coil Products at roughly US$461 million and BasX at about US$535 million, partly offset by US$199 million of eliminations between segments. AAON’s market cap is around US$6.5b, putting it in mid to large cap territory.

Investors watching the AI data center freight story may want AAON on their radar because BasX branded data center solutions and high efficiency rooftop units are tied directly to the heavy HVAC boxes that fill those new server halls, feeding ongoing trucking needs while projects are built out. The company has pointed to a sizable backlog, new capacity in Memphis and interest in liquid and air side cooling for denser AI facilities. These factors together could support future earnings if orders flow through cleanly. At the same time, AAON is working through ERP and capacity ramp issues, carries meaningful capital spending and has seen margins under pressure, so any stumble in execution or a pause in data center build plans could have a negative impact. For investors comfortable with that trade off, AAON offers a focused way to follow how AI driven cooling demand and construction freight translate into future cash and earnings quality.

nVent Electric (NVT)

nVent Electric supplies the electrical enclosures, power connections and cooling systems that sit around data centers and other critical infrastructure, which helps explain its link to construction freight and heavy equipment moves in this screener. The business is split between Systems Protection, which generated about US$3.4b of revenue, and Electrical Connections at roughly US$1.4b. This gives investors a clear view of how it earns money from protecting and connecting power and data. nVent Electric has a market cap of about US$25.3b, putting it firmly in large cap territory.

Investors watching the AI data center freight theme may find nVent Electric hard to ignore because it sells the physical gear that goes onto flatbeds, into modular outdoor enclosures and across rural job sites as power hungry facilities are built out. Management has talked about record orders, a growing backlog and new liquid cooling capacity that tie directly to data center projects. The planned Maverick Power deal would deepen its role in power distribution for those sites. The flip side is meaningful reliance on AI related capex, a premium valuation and a funding mix tilted toward external borrowing, so any pause in data center build plans or tighter credit conditions could hit expectations faster than some investors anticipate.
